<reason>CON opened very strongly by turning every PRO example into a case for physical crowd management and pressing the "same feet, worse information" and enforceability lines. But PRO progressively narrowed the clash to a defensible reading of the motion ("destinations should limit" via de-promotion, platform partnerships, permits) and used its pressure question to extract CON's concession that own-channel de-promotion and platform pin-pauses are fine. CON's rejoinder—that this reading is toothless/unfalsifiable and that voluntary norms "suffice without the motion"—largely restates the motion rather than opposing it, and CON's use of Jackson Hole as proof that voluntary de-promotion kept trails open actually supports PRO's effectiveness claim. CON's "recruitment is not arrival" and capacity-rationing points remained live, and the "real but marginal" concession on aggregation was reasonable, but PRO's prevention-versus-response frame (gates bury the last crowd; pin limits blunt the next) plus its answer to the prediction-symmetry point (no forecast needed to pull a pin the morning a spike appears; platforms act in hours, gates take a season) gave the third-party reader the cleaner reason to vote. Competitive but PRO made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B3.1/B4.2/B5.4 sequence: asking what word of the motion CON actually opposes once a destination de-promotes its own feed and asks platforms to pause the pin, then converting CON's "editorial discretion is fine" answer into the closing charge that CON's remaining objection is to a mandate the motion never requires.</best_rebuttal>
